system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2191-03-21 21:01:00 to 2191-03-22 15:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, a history of two kidney transplants, and a recent UTI was admitted for hyperglycemia and mild diabetic ketoacidosis. She presented with blood glucose in the 400s, abdominal pain, nausea, and trace ketones. She was treated with IV fluids and an insulin drip, which resolved the DKA. Her insulin pump was restarted with adjusted basal rates to prevent recurrence. During admission, she had a troponin rise peaking at 0.94 ng/mL without symptoms or EKG changes, consistent with a type 2 NSTEMI likely due to metabolic stress from DKA and hypovolemia. She continued treatment for a complicated UTI with cefpodoxime, and her renal transplant function improved with hydration. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans to follow up with endocrinology and cardiology.
problems: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming by. I’ve been feeling off for a while, but my blood sugars were in the 400s this week. I think I accidentally used my old insulin pump site after my shower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That could definitely cause high blood sugars. We checked your labs in the ER, and your glucose was 259 when you arrived, down from higher levels. We’ve already switched your pump to a fresh site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I keep the old site just in case the new one fails, but I must’ve mixed them up. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. Insulin doesn’t absorb well from old sites, so even if the pump is working, you’re not getting the dose you need. That’s why your sugars spiked and you had some ketones at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had DKA before when this happened. I didn’t want to wait this time, so I called my endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We gave you some fluids and monitored your levels. Your blood work shows your acid levels are normalizing. No signs of DKA now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been urinating a lot—was that from the high sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. When blood sugar is high, your body tries to get rid of the extra glucose through urine. We tested your urine and found no infection, so it’s likely just from the diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it was another UTI, especially with my transplant history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re always cautious with that, but your labs don’t show infection. Your kidney function is actually improving—creatinine is down to 1.0 from 1.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been stressed lately—being a single mom and managing all these appointments is overwhelming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We noted your mood during the exam. It’s a lot to handle. We’ll make sure your follow-up is coordinated so it’s easier on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your overnight labs look great—glucose was 79 this morning, and your electrolytes are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Is everything back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. One thing—we checked your thyroid level and it was a bit low, so we’re reducing your levothyroxine from 112 to 100 mcg daily. Please follow up with your PCP to recheck it in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make that appointment. And I’ll stick with the new pump site—no more old ones!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Keep monitoring your sugars, take all your meds—including your transplant and diabetes ones—and we’ll send the discharge summary to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the nurse go over your discharge instructions, and you should be able to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. Blood sugars are staying around 110, and I’m not feeling tired anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to follow up with your endocrinologist and primary care doctor, especially for the thyroid change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’re here if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge paperwork is ready. You can head home anytime now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I really appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Stay safe, and take care of yourself and your son.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, kidney transplant status, and multiple comorbidities was admitted for hyperglycemia caused by accidental use of an old insulin pump site. She presented with elevated blood glucose and a history of malaise and urinary frequency. In the hospital, her insulin pump site was replaced, leading to rapid improvement in glucose control. Labs showed resolution of any metabolic imbalance, and urine testing ruled out infection. Her thyroid function was found to be over-replaced, so her levothyroxine dose was reduced at discharge. She was medically stable, back to baseline, and discharged home with instructions to continue proper pump site management and follow up with her primary care and endocrinology providers.
